summary: This work demonstrates driven-dissipative entanglement generation in a superconducting waveguide-QED system using two giant atoms (transmon qubits coupled twice to a common waveguide). The protocol exploits correlated dissipation and interference at multiple coupling points to autonomously stabilize a Bell state with fidelity $F = 0.89 \pm 0.02$, followed by frequency tuning to suppress individual dissipation for readout.
motivation: Driven-dissipative protocols offer an alternative to pulse-calibrated coherent schemes for remote entanglement generation, but dissipation that enables entanglement usually corrupts it during readout. Giant-atom interference effects enable tunable individual and collective dissipation to overcome this fundamental limitation.
method: Two transmon qubits are coupled sequentially to a waveguide at $\gamma(\omega_\mathrm{super})/2\pi \approx 14.7$ MHz per coupling point. A continuous drive at frequency $\omega_d = \omega_\mathrm{super}$ with amplitude $\Omega/2\pi = 45$ MHz and detuning $\delta/2\pi = 6.81$ MHz for duration $\tau = 1.5$ µs stabilizes the triplet state $|\Psi^+\rangle$ via correlated dissipation; afterward, qubits are flux-tuned to the subradiant frequency $\omega_\mathrm{sub}/2\pi = 4.66$ GHz to decouple from the waveguide ($\Gamma/2\pi \approx 5.4$ kHz) and preserve entanglement for tomography.
result: Bell-state fidelity $F = 0.89 \pm 0.02$ and concurrence $C = 0.86 \pm 0.02$ are achieved; the dark-state stabilization timescale is $\tau_S \approx 159$ ns and dark-state lifetime $\tau_D \approx 99.6$ ns. Infidelity sources: finite drive strength (4.7%), leakage to transmon $|f\rangle$ state (2.9%), pure dephasing (1.8%), non-radiative decay (0.5%).
